title: Determinant over GF(p): cofactor expansion vs Gaussian elimination
problem_statement: Given an n x n matrix A with entries in the prime field GF(p), p = 2^31 - 1 (entries given as integers in [0, p)), compute det(A) mod p, returned as an integer in [0, p). The determinant of the 0 x 0 matrix is 1.

input.size_measure: n^2 field elements of 31 bits each. p is fixed, so every field operation (add, multiply, and inversion by O(log p) = O(1) multiplications) is unit cost.

algorithms.name: Laplace (cofactor) expansion
algorithms.idea: Expand along the first row: det(A) = sum_j (-1)^j A[0][j] det(minor(0, j)), recursively, without reusing any minor.
algorithms.pseudocode: expand(r, cols): if r == n return 1; return sum over k-th c in cols of (-1)^k A[r][c] * expand(r+1, cols - {c})
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n!) field operations (n!/k! recursion nodes with k columns left, Theta(k^2) work each; n! * sum_k k^2/k! = Theta(n!)); exactly floor(e n!) - 1 multiplications for n >= 1 (PROOFS.md section 1)
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n^2) (recursion depth n, a column list of length <= n per level)
algorithms.correctness: Laplace's expansion along the first row, proved from the Leibniz formula det(A) = sum over permutations s of sgn(s) prod_i A[i][s(i)] in PROOFS.md section 1 (valid over any commutative ring). Expanding fully gives the Leibniz formula term by term.

algorithms.name: Gaussian elimination mod p
algorithms.idea: Reduce A to upper-triangular form with row swaps (each negates the determinant) and row operations row_r -= f * row_c (which preserve it); the determinant is the signed product of the pivots. A column with no non-zero pivot candidate means det = 0.
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^3) field operations on non-singular input: exactly (n^3 - n)/3 multiply-subtracts (~n^3/3), n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 multiplications in all and n inversions (PROOFS.md section 2); O(n^3) always (it can stop early on a singular matrix)
algorithms.correctness: Proof: PROOFS.md section 2. Adding a multiple of one row to another leaves det unchanged, swapping two rows negates it, the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal, and a column without a pivot makes the matrix singular. GF(p) is a field (p = 2^31 - 1 is prime), so every non-zero pivot is invertible (Fermat: x^(p-2) = x^(-1)).

relationship: Factorial -> cubic: Theta(n!) vs Theta(n^3) field operations. The expansion ignores that det is invariant under row operations; elimination exploits it. Faster algorithms through fast matrix multiplication, a further T3 step, are listed under background (cited, not proved here).

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree for n = 0..8 (cofactor expansion capped at n = 8), and both match the determinant known by construction: the harness builds A as a row-permuted L*U with unit lower triangular L, so det(A) = sign(permutation) * prod(diag U) mod p, independent of both implementations. Instances include zero entries (zero pivots, row swaps) and singular matrices (a zero on U's diagonal); n = 12 and 30 are checked for Gaussian elimination only. V2: runtimes fitted against n! and n^3, on uniformly random matrices (non-singular with probability at least 1 - 1/(p - 1), PROOFS.md section 4.2) for the timing. tests/test_proofs_determinant.py checks the exact operation counts of PROOFS.md (cofactor expansion n = 0..8, elimination n = 0..40) and both algorithms against the Leibniz formula.

caveats: Working over GF(p) with p fixed makes every arithmetic step unit cost. Integer matrices are a different setting (see background for Bareiss's fraction-free elimination). Gaussian elimination over floating point is a different (numerical) problem and is not what is measured here.
notes: Contrast with permanent-naive-vs-ryser: the permanent is the same sum over permutations with the signs removed; the exact algorithms of that entry take Theta(n * n!) and Theta(n 2^n) operations, and computing it is #P-complete (background). The signs are what make det invariant under row operations (PROOFS.md section 2.1), which is what elimination exploits; the permanent has no such invariance (permanent-naive-vs-ryser/PROOFS.md, section 5.5).

background.statement: With fast matrix multiplication the determinant can be computed in O(n^omega) field operations, via LUP decomposition; this is a further T3 step.
Strassen's algorithm gives omega <= log2(7), so the determinant takes O(n^log2(7)) operations.
The matrix multiplication exponent satisfies omega < 2.371339.
background.source: Alman, Duan, Vassilevska Williams, Xu, Xu & Zhou 2024 (SODA 2025)

background.statement: Over the integers, Bareiss's multistep integer-preserving Gaussian elimination, based on Sylvester's identity, avoids fractions.
